newsitem.title: USA: Drop in welfare cases due to economy, laws - U.S. study.
newsitem.headline: Drop in welfare cases due to economy, laws - U.S. study.

text.p: A growing economy and tougher state laws were the main reasons for a sharp drop in welfare cases in recent years, a White House study said on Friday.
From January 1993 to January 1997 the number of people receiving welfare in the United States fell by 20 percent, or 2.75 million recipients. Caseloads were at a historic high in 1993.

Fully 44 percent of the decline in welfare rolls across the nation during that period was due to an expanding economy and falling unemployment rate, President Bill Clinton's Council of Economic Advisers said in a report.

Federal waivers allowing states to experiment with new approaches to welfare accounted for roughly another third of the decline. Other factors, such as an expansion of federal tax breaks for the working poor, may account for the rest, the report said.
The study gave no indication what happened to individuals who left the welfare rolls, saying additional research was needed to determine the practical effect of dramatic changes in welfare policy.

Clinton last year signed a sweeping welfare law that ends the federal guarantee of aid for poor women and children, replacing it with block grants to states. Federal benefits are limited to five years, and most recipients are required to work after two years.

Before the law was signed, the White House approved special waivers allowing more than 40 states to experiment with their own welfare changes, including limits on aid, work requirements and other reforms.
